Nell had signed up for the election committee in September, before anyone knew who would run, because it got her out of study hall on Fridays. By October the job had a shape: two candidates for seventh-grade representative, a ballot box made from a shoe box and packing tape, and one rule, printed in Ms. Okafor's neat capitals across the top of the tally sheet: A VOTE COUNTS ONLY IF THE VOTER'S CHOICE IS CLEAR.

The candidates were Owen Park, who had promised a longer lunch period, and June Albright, who had sat beside Nell on the bus every morning since third grade. Nell had listened to June practice her speech on that bus for a week, until June could say the first line without looking at her card. On Tuesday, before the box was taped shut, Nell had voted for her.

On Wednesday afternoon, in the empty library, Nell unfolded the ballots one at a time and read each name aloud. Ms. Okafor made a mark on the tally sheet for every name, and Theo Brandt, the other committee member, kept a second sheet to check hers. About two-thirds of the way through, Nell unfolded a ballot and stopped. Someone had made a large, hurried check mark. It began in the box beside June's name, and its long tail ran up across the line and into the box beside Owen's.

"Set it to one side," Ms. Okafor said. "We'll come back to it at the end."

At the end, both sheets agreed. Owen had fifty-nine votes and June had fifty-eight, and the one ballot lay by itself on the table.

Ms. Okafor turned it to face Nell. "You've read every ballot," she said. "Tell us what you see."

Nell looked at it for a long time. The check began on June's side; anyone could see that. A voter in a hurry might start a check in the right box and let the pen run on. But a voter might also start in one box, change their mind halfway, and drag the pen toward the other. She thought of June on the bus, saying her first line over and over. Then she read the sentence across the top of the tally sheet again.

"I can't tell which one they meant," she said.

Theo nodded. Ms. Okafor wrote SPOILED across the back of the ballot, clipped it to the tally sheet, and signed her name under the totals.

The winner's name was read over the speakers before the last bell, and by the next morning June had heard. She slid into the bus seat beside Nell. "Was it close?"

"One vote."

June looked out the window. "Did you have to throw any out?"

"One," Nell said. She had slept badly, going over what she would say when June asked which box the check had started in.

June asked nothing more. She took out her math notebook, found her page, and said, without looking up, "I'm glad it was you counting."

Under each swing in the park on Delaney Street
the ground is worn into a bowl,
a hollow about the length of a shoe's long drag,
deepest just where the seat hangs lowest.

Nobody dug it. It was dug
by a few thousand small decisions to slow down:
sneakers scuffed at the bottom of an arc,
a boot heel planted, a sandal dragged,

a girl who meant to jump and then, at the last,
chose to stay, and set her feet.
Each of them moved a spoonful of dirt,
or less, a pinch, a crumb,

and went off to the slide or the gate or home
and left the rest of the work to whoever came next.
In April the hollows hold rain,
and sparrows drop down to bathe in them

as if somebody had built them a row of basins.
In August the dirt in them is soft as flour.
Twice the city has sent a truck of wood chips
to fill them level with the rest of the yard,

and twice, by the end of summer, the bowls came back,
scuffed out a crumb at a time
by children who knew nothing of the trucks,
only that a swing has to stop somewhere.

This year I bring my nephew, who is four
and whose toes have just begun to reach the ground.
He pumps and leans and pumps, and when he wants to stop
he drags his feet, and the swing shudders,

and he looks down at the little cloud of dust
rising out of the bowl into the light
as though he had made the whole thing himself.
I let him think so. In a way, he has.

The summer I was twelve, my aunt, who looked after me on weeknights while my mother worked, signed me up for the handbell choir at the community center, mostly because it met on Tuesday evenings and so did her pottery class. I had never held a handbell. I assumed it would be like playing the piano, only louder.

There were eleven of us, standing in a row behind long tables padded with foam and covered in black cloth. Mrs. Halloran, the director, handed me two bells, an F and the G just above it, and a pair of white cotton gloves. The gloves, she said, kept the oil from our fingers off the brass. Then she showed me how to ring: lift the bell to the shoulder, swing it forward in a small arc, and let the clapper strike once. To stop the sound, you pressed the rim against your chest.

I had expected to play songs. Instead I played two notes, and only when their turn came. The music for the whole choir was printed on one page, and I followed my two lines with a pencil, counting the rests between them under my breath. Sometimes I waited twelve beats for a single F. Mrs. Vance, beside me, rang the A and the B-flat; the man beside her rang the next two notes up. Each of us held a few notes, and none of us held the tune.

For the first month I could hear only my own bells and the silence around them. I listened for my place, rang my F, damped it against my shirt, and started counting again. When Mrs. Halloran said that we were sounding better, I took her word for it. I had no idea what we sounded like.

The concert was in October, in the center's gym, with folding chairs for about sixty people. In the third piece, a slow arrangement of "Shenandoah," I lost my count during a long rest. I knew a G was coming, but the numbers in my head had come loose from the music, and I stood with the bell raised and my face hot. Then Mrs. Vance, without turning her head, tapped two fingers twice on the edge of the table, so lightly that only the ringers nearest her could have noticed. On the second tap I rang, and the G came out exactly where it belonged.

Afterward my aunt played me the recording she had made on her phone. I listened for my two bells and could barely pick them out. What I heard instead was "Shenandoah," whole and slow, the tune passing from one pair of hands to the next down the row so smoothly that it might have been a single instrument. Somewhere inside it was a G that had come out on time because of two taps.

I rang with the choir for four more years. By the end I could hear the whole tune while I played, and I watched the ringer beside me as closely as I watched the page. In my last year a new boy stood at my old place with the F and the G. During his first concert, in the middle of a long rest, I saw his lips stop moving, and I tapped twice on the table.

Until 1809 the village of Caddow, in the hill country of Orrin County, had no regular mail. A letter for Caddow traveled as far as the county seat at Varrick, eighteen miles south, and waited in a box at the courthouse until someone from the village happened to ride down on business and carried it home. In a dry summer that might happen every week. In mud season it might take a month.

In 1808 the state approved a post road from Varrick north to the river crossing at Sayer's Ferry, and the road commissioners sent a surveyor named Josiah Crane to lay out the route. The people of Caddow expected the road to climb the hill to their green, where the meetinghouse, the store, and a dozen houses stood around a square of grass. Crane walked the hill. Then he walked the flat land along Tarrant Brook, a mile to the east, and drew the road along the brook. A road over the hill, he wrote in his report, would climb two hundred feet and come down again only to visit one village, while on the flats a loaded wagon could keep moving all day.

The village sent the commissioners a petition, signed by forty-one men, asking that the line be moved. It was read, entered in the record, and set aside. The road was finished along the brook in the fall of 1809, and a rider began carrying mail up it every Thursday.

The post office went where the road went. Eli Thorne, who had opened a small tavern where the new road crossed the old cart track up to Caddow, was named postmaster, and he kept the mail in a cabinet behind his bar. In those years postage was often paid by the person who received a letter rather than the one who sent it, so every Thursday evening Thorne's tavern filled with people collecting letters and counting out coins, and many of them stayed for supper.

Within a few years the store followed. Its owner, Ruth Ames, took the building apart board by board in the spring of 1814 and put it back together across the road from the tavern. A blacksmith came next, then a harness maker, then a second store. By 1830 the cluster of buildings had a name of its own, Caddow Crossing, and more people lived there than on the hill.

The meetinghouse stayed where it was. For another forty years families went up the hill on Sundays and down to the crossing for everything else. In 1851 the town meeting voted to build a town hall and, after a long argument, built it at the crossing, beside the road. A few years later the old green was sold as pasture.

The hill is still called Old Caddow, and a stone marks the corner where the meetinghouse stood. The road along the brook is paved now and carries a state route number, but people in town still call it the Post Road. Few of them know that the center of their town was chosen by a surveyor who was thinking about wagons.

item.passage:
When an earthquake strikes, the shaking does not reach every place at the same moment. The sudden slip of rock along a fault, often many kilometers underground, sends out several kinds of waves, and they travel through the Earth at different speeds. That difference turns out to be one of the most useful facts in the study of earthquakes. It lets scientists find where an earthquake began using only instruments hundreds of kilometers away.

The fastest waves are called primary waves, or P waves. They push and pull on the rock in the direction they are traveling, squeezing and stretching it, much as a pulse travels along a stretched spring when one end is given a shove. In the rock of the upper crust they move at roughly six kilometers per second. Behind them come secondary waves, or S waves, which shake the rock from side to side, at right angles to their direction of travel, like the wave that runs along a rope when one end is flicked. S waves move at a little more than half the speed of P waves.

A seismograph close to an earthquake records the two kinds of waves arriving almost together. A station farther away records the P waves first, then a pause, then the S waves, and the pause grows longer with distance, for the same reason that two runners who start together finish farther apart in a longer race. For earthquakes within a few hundred kilometers, seismologists use a rough rule: the distance to the source is roughly eight kilometers for each second of delay between the P and S waves.

From the delay alone, one station can tell how far away an earthquake was, but not in which direction. The source could lie anywhere on a circle around the station. A second station adds a second circle, and two circles usually cross at two points. A third circle settles the question: the point where all three meet marks the epicenter, the spot on the surface above where the rock first slipped. Computers now do this with readings from many stations at once, but the idea is the one seismologists once worked out by hand with compasses and paper maps.

The gap between the two waves has revealed more than the locations of earthquakes. S waves are unable to pass through a liquid, which flows aside instead of springing back when it is pushed sideways. In the early twentieth century, seismologists found that S waves from large earthquakes failed to reach a broad band of stations on the far side of the planet from the source. The likeliest explanation was that something deep inside the Earth was stopping them, and this became some of the earliest evidence that the Earth's outer core is liquid.

The gap also has a practical use. P waves arrive first and usually do little damage, so a network of sensors that detects them can send out a warning before the stronger shaking of the S waves and the slower waves behind them arrives. The warning is short, usually a few seconds and rarely much more than a minute, and places very close to the source may get none at all. Still, a few seconds can be enough to slow a train, open the doors of a fire station, or let a student get under a desk.
